method: Three independent superforecaster panelists per target (outside-view / unit-economics / contrarian lens). Binary targets aggregated as extremized median (extremization factor 1.73); quantity targets as median of points with median CI bounds. Panel disagreement is reported, not hidden.

thesis_propositions.statement: Frontier model training is a large fixed cost (R&D/capex, independent of revenue, amortized over multi-year horizons), while inference is a real marginal cost (COGS) that scales roughly linearly with usage/revenue — unlike classic zero-marginal-cost software.
thesis_propositions.testable_via: Lab financial disclosures and credible leaks (OpenAI/Anthropic training-compute R&D vs. inference COGS lines); hyperscaler capex and GPU depreciation schedules (3-6 year lives vs. actual useful life); SemiAnalysis-style TCO models splitting training vs. serving cost; test whether reported inference cost tracks token volume ~1:1 while training spend is invariant to revenue.

thesis_propositions.statement: US inference is currently supply-constrained, and demand is concentrated on OpenAI and Anthropic, giving them pricing power: their per-token prices sit well above the marginal cost of serving (a scarcity 'price umbrella', with markups cascading from Nvidia through compute resellers to labs).
thesis_propositions.testable_via: Estimate marginal serving cost per million tokens for comparable-size models on rented GPU capacity (e.g., cost to serve a Kimi K3-class model on Together/Fireworks/hyperscaler H100/B200 rates) and compare to OpenAI/Anthropic list prices; evidence of rationing (rate limits, capacity-constrained statements on earnings calls, enterprise waitlists); implied inference gross margins from disclosed revenue and compute contracts.

thesis_propositions.statement: Chinese open-weight token prices are set near the marginal cost of inference because open weights allow competitive third-party hosting (the marginal supplier prices at marginal cost); therefore the US-China price gap measures the US scarcity premium, not a structural Chinese cost advantage — Thompson doubts Chinese inference is cheaper on a true marginal-cost basis.
thesis_propositions.testable_via: Price dispersion across independent hosts serving the identical open-weight model (competition should compress hosting margins to near zero); implied gross margins of open-model hosts vs. closed labs; input-cost parity checks (GPU rental and electricity in China vs. US, effect of export-controlled chips on Chinese cost per token) to see whether Chinese serving cost is actually equal or higher.

thesis_propositions.statement: Chinese open-source labs eat or externalize the fixed cost of training: distillation of US frontier model outputs lowers their training bill, and monetization runs through adjacent channels (Alibaba cloud/ecosystem, robotics/manufacturing adoption, state strategic goals) rather than token margins.
thesis_propositions.testable_via: Technical evidence of distillation (output-similarity and model-fingerprinting studies, lab accusations with data); reported training budgets of Kimi/Qwen/DeepSeek vs. US frontier runs of comparable capability; business-model analysis showing Chinese labs' revenue is attributed to cloud/ecosystem rather than API token margins; policy statements (e.g., Xi-era open-weight encouragement) as corroborating motive.

thesis_propositions.statement: When US compute supply catches up with demand, US token prices converge toward marginal cost and the price umbrella collapses: constant-quality inference prices should fall materially as datacenter capacity comes online, and price cuts should correlate with supply additions (and competitive open-weight releases) rather than cost declines alone.
thesis_propositions.testable_via: Time series of frontier API prices per constant-quality unit (price per benchmark-equivalent completed task, not per raw token) against capacity additions (datacenter GW energized, GPU shipment volumes); event studies around large capacity blocks coming online or major open-weight releases; whether OpenAI/Anthropic gross margins on inference compress as constraint eases.

thesis_propositions.statement: Per-token price comparisons are misleading because tokens are not a commodity (different models consume different token counts for the same task — intelligence is the commoditizing unit); as prices converge, capex payback depends on differentiation via lowest cost-per-unit-of-intelligence (token efficiency, serving scale) and up-stack product integration (e.g., Claude Code), which Thompson expects but does not guarantee will save the frontier labs.
thesis_propositions.testable_via: Benchmark cost-per-completed-task across models (tokens consumed x price for identical task suites) to test whether nominally cheaper Chinese models are cheaper per outcome; retention/switching data for integrated products (Claude Code, ChatGPT apps) vs. raw API usage under price pressure; payback modeling of training capex under converged-price scenarios (does amortization complete before commoditization?); market share of labs with lowest cost-per-task as prices fall.

forecasts.question: Will the 2024-2026 US AI capex vintage (hyperscaler + lab data-center/compute investment committed in those years) earn back at least its cost of capital by end of 2030? Operationalize: by end-2030, is aggregate AI-attributable revenue running at a level that credible analyses judge sufficient to cover depreciation + cost of capital on that vintage — i.e., mainstream analyst consensus says the vintage was NPV-positive, not written down.

panel.reasoning:
Outside view first. Peak-and-near-peak vintages of hype-driven general-purpose-technology infrastructure booms have earned their cost of capital within ~5 years in roughly 2 of 10 historical cases (UK rail 1844-47, US rail 1880s, 1920s utilities, telecom/fiber 1998-2001, 3G spectrum, Chinese solar, US shale, streaming content). The counter-class - cash-rich incumbents expanding into a proven, sold-out adjacency (AWS/Azure/GCP 2012-2020, Amazon fulfillment, datacenter REITs, TSMC leading edge) - pays back ~70% of the time. The 2024-2026 US AI vintage splits roughly 40-45% into the incumbent class (hyperscaler capacity against contracted backlog, plus power/shell/land which is ~40% of capex, long-lived and genuinely scarce) and 55-60% into the mania/short-life class (accelerators on 5-6yr books but ~3-4yr frontier lives, neocloud/SPV/lab-directed builds, vendor-financed circularity). Blended base rate ~30-35%, and lower for a binary aggregate verdict than for the dollar share, since the good half must carry the bad half.

Fermi: US AI-attributable capex committed 2024-2026 is roughly $1.05-1.2T (2024 ~$160B, 2025 ~$340B, 2026 ~$550-600B). At a blended ~7-year economic life (58% at 5yr, 42% at 15yr) and 10% WACC, the annuity charge is ~$225B/yr, implying ~$300-330B/yr of sustained AI-attributable revenue against this fleet - about $420B/yr if Epoch/Amazon/Burry are right that true economic life is 3-4 years. Exiting-2026 end-customer AI revenue is ~$180-250B annualized, maybe $150-200B net of intra-industry double counting, so ~30%/yr growth is needed while 2027-2030 vintages with better perf-per-dollar compete for the same tokens. Same order as Cahn ($1.5T/yr) and Bain ($800B/yr shortfall). Structural estimate 30-38%; reconciled prior ~33%.

Bayesian update with clustered likelihood ratios: positive cluster LR ~2.2 (still supply-constrained after tripling capex three years running, $514B Google RPO, rentals re-tightening to $2.35, Anthropic $1B to $47B run-rate with >70% inference margins and a first operating profit, power scarcity rents, and demand elasticity that has so far exceeded 10-50x/yr constant-quality price deflation - the key empirical break from fiber); supply-catch-up/obsolescence cluster LR ~0.50 (new H100 deployments already NPV-negative on short contracts, 60-80% peak-to-trough rental decline, ~3-4yr frontier lifespan vs 5-6yr books - Thompson's T5 already visible one layer below tokens); demand-disappointment cluster LR ~0.60 (OpenAI cutting 2030 compute from $1.4T commitments to $600-750B, missing early-2026 targets, losing $20.9B on $13.1B revenue; the revenue-gap literature is literally the 'credible analysis' the resolution criterion invokes); financing-fragility cluster LR ~0.80 (Oracle/neocloud/SPV/private credit plus Nvidia-to-OpenAI vendor financing, the Lucent/Global Crossing pattern, raising the odds of visible write-downs in the aggregate). That yields ~21%.

Resolution-criterion correction pushes up: consensus verdicts are pro-cyclical, follow stock prices, and are lenient toward incumbents who control the reporting and can extend lives instead of impairing. A scenario decomposition (P(AI trade visibly working in 2030) ~0.475 x P(consensus affirms | working) ~0.75, plus bust branch at ~0.08) gives ~40%. I weight the mechanism estimate more heavily because the criterion requires an affirmative aggregate verdict, and the modal in-between world - hyperscalers fine, periphery impaired, dueling analyses - resolves No.

Key discipline point against 'this time is different': in fiber, rail and shale, mid-boom volume validation was always real; the failures were price failures. Thompson's thesis is a price thesis, so exploding token volumes and lab run-rates are not evidence against the reference class. The genuine differences that do earn an upward adjustment are (a) the spenders are self-funded incumbents with contracted, paying backlogs rather than levered speculative entrants, (b) unit-level inference margins are already positive and improving, and (c) the binding constraint is power, a scarce long-lived asset. The 2024 slice (~14% of dollars) has likely already paid back at umbrella prices; the 2026 slice (~56%) deploys into the consensus 2028 oversupply window and drives the verdict. Dollar-weighted central payback ratio ~0.98x with a fat left tail.

Final: 0.27, with an 80% interval of 0.13-0.46 reflecting both real-world uncertainty and material ambiguity in how a 2030 judge would read 'mainstream analyst consensus'.
reference_classes: Hype-driven general-purpose-technology infrastructure buildouts, peak/near-peak vintage: UK railway mania 1844-47, US railroads 1880s, 1920s electric utility holding companies, telecom/fiber 1998-2001, European 3G spectrum 2000, Chinese solar 2010-12, US shale 2011-15, streaming content spend 2019-22 (~20% earned cost of capital within ~5 years)

Cash-rich incumbents expanding capex into an already-profitable, demonstrably sold-out adjacency: AWS/Azure/GCP 2012-2020, Amazon fulfillment 2015-19, datacenter REITs 2015-23, TSMC leading-edge fabs 2016-23 (~70% payback)

Short-lived, rapidly obsoleting assets purchased at scarcity prices: DRAM/foundry capacity at cycle peaks, GPU mining rigs 2017 and 2021, dry-bulk/tanker orders at peak charter rates (~20-25% payback for peak vintage)
Vendor-financed / circular-revenue booms: Lucent and Nortel customer financing 1999-2001, dot-com infrastructure purchased with VC money (near-universal capital impairment)

How mainstream analyst consensus retrospectively judges large capex vintages 4-6 years later: cloud 2014-16 judged clearly positive, Meta Reality Labs judged clearly negative, telecom 1999-2001 judged catastrophic - the criterion cleanly separates these worlds
Perez installation-vs-deployment phase framework: installation-phase capital typically impaired even when the technology succeeds
key_uncertainties: Demand elasticity (Thompson's own flagged uncertainty): whether aggregate AI revenue keeps compounding faster than constant-quality price deflation. So far it has - the single biggest break from the fiber analogy - but fiber's revenue also grew until it abruptly did not.

Timing of US compute supply catching demand. Analyst consensus clusters on 2028 broad oversupply; if it slips to 2030+ the vintage earns umbrella rents for most of its life, if it arrives in 2027 the ~56% of dollars committed in 2026 are impaired.

True economic life of 2024-2026 accelerators: 5-6 years as booked, or 3-4 years as Epoch's frontier-lifespan data, Amazon's 2025 shortening, and Burry's $176B claim imply. This alone swings the required annual revenue by ~40%.

How much of current AI revenue is circular (lab revenue funded by strategic investors and vendor financing) versus genuine external enterprise/consumer willingness to pay. Enterprise ROI evidence remains weak relative to token growth.

OpenAI's trajectory specifically: it cut its 2030 compute plan from $1.4T of headline commitments to ~$600-750B and missed early-2026 revenue targets while losing $20.9B on $13.1B. As the largest single demand source, a restructuring of its commitments would resolve much of the question.

Resolution ambiguity: 'mainstream analyst consensus says NPV-positive, not written down' is a fuzzy aggregate verdict. Consensus follows stock prices and hyperscalers can extend useful lives rather than impair, creating a 'cheap yes' channel; conversely an ambiguous middling world defaults to No.
Whether the ~40% of capex in power, shells, land and interconnection (scarce, long-lived, 55-month ERCOT queues) earns enough rent to carry the impaired accelerator half.

Composition drift toward debt: Oracle, neoclouds, SPVs and private credit are an increasing share of the 2026 slice, raising the probability of visible headline write-downs even in a moderately successful scenario.

panel.reasoning:
UNIT ECONOMICS DRIVE THE ANSWER. Size the vintage: US AI-attributable DC capex 2024 ~$215B + 2025 ~$450B + 2026 ~$850B = ~$1.5T (+/-$0.3T), weighted 14/30/56 — so the 2026 tranche dominates. Mix is 58% short-lived IT ($0.87T) / 42% shell-power-land ($0.63T). Required annual return at zero NPV via capital-recovery factor at 9.5% blended WACC: IT CRF 0.241 = $210B/yr, shell CRF 0.110 = $69B/yr, total ~$279B/yr net cash flow; at ~72% cash margin that is ~$390B/yr of infra-level revenue for ~6 years (~$2.8T lifetime gross). Grossed up through the lab/app stack: ~$700-800B/yr of end-user AI revenue. Triangulates against Cahn (~$1.5T/yr, stricter — he demands ~1-yr payback with margin) and Bain ($2T/yr by 2030, pro-rated to this $1.5T slice of a ~$5-6T cumulative buildout = $500-600B/yr): three paths within ~1.5x.

Against actual: ~$180-230B end-user run-rate exiting 2026 (Anthropic $47B, OpenAI ~$25-30B, MSFT AI $37B, GCP/AWS AI, app layer, net of double-counting). Reaching ~$750B by 2030 needs only a 35-40% CAGR — far below the current 150-400%/yr lab and 50-80%/yr AI-cloud trajectories. That bar is forgiving.

THE BEAR DCF THAT NEARLY KILLED IT: valuing the vintage at merchant spot rates with revenue share decaying 95% (2026) to 19% (2030) as $3-5T of 3-10x-more-efficient silicon arrives yields only ~$1.15T lifetime gross vs the ~$2.8T requirement — deeply NPV-negative. Two corrections rescue it. (1) Much of the vintage is CONTRACTED, not merchant: Google's $514B backlog, Oracle RPO, Microsoft's ~$80B unfulfillable backlog, CoreWeave's book, Anthropic's $185B and OpenAI's ~$1.25T of commitments. Take-or-pay struck at 2025-26 scarcity prices locks the umbrella in for the asset owner's full economic life and transfers convergence risk to the labs — confirmed empirically by CoreWeave's 2020-vintage A100s still fully contracted and H100s re-signed at ~95% of original price. This is what Thompson's framework understates: umbrella collapse hits token SELLERS, not contracted compute OWNERS. (2) ~22% is Google/Meta first-party earning ad-margin returns on a defended $450B+ franchise, not rental rates.

Re-decomposed by owner/mechanism: first-party ads 22% at P=0.72; merchant-contracted 60% at P=0.58; lab-owned (OpenAI/xAI) 18% at P=0.40 -> weighted 0.578. Cross-check by sub-vintage (2024 Hopper already at cash payback — ~$40-50k net cash per GPU over 2.3 yrs vs $45-50k all-in — P=0.85; 2025 P=0.70; 2026 P=0.50) gives 0.61. Reconciled ~0.59.

OUTSIDE VIEW: 12 comparable capex vintages give a ~40% base rate; early-vintage subclass ~50-52%. The discriminator separating PASS from FAIL is utilization/price direction at peak build. Fiber at peak build had ~3% lit capacity and collapsing prices; AI at peak build (mid-2026) has rationed sold-out capacity, H100 rentals UP 38%, API list prices UP 4x, and a $514B backlog. Diametrically opposite the canonical failure case.

BAYESIAN CHAIN from 0.52: +2026 price increases as $850B of supply lands (LR 2.5, falsifies near-term umbrella collapse) -> 0.73; +Anthropic first operating profit at >70% inference GM (LR 1.5, discounted for run-rate vs recognized) -> 0.80; -OpenAI cutting 2030 compute $1.4T to $600-750B and missing targets (LR 0.54) -> 0.69; -OpenAI $20.9B operating loss (LR 0.64) -> 0.585; -SemiAnalysis negative-NPV new H100 (LR 0.64) -> 0.475; +power as structural umbrella protection, ERCOT 143.5GW queue vs 85.9GW peak with 55-mo waits, making 42% of the vintage an appreciating asset (LR 1.67) -> 0.60; +chip cascade evidence (LR 1.4) -> 0.68; -revenue-gap literature already mainstream (LR 0.67) -> 0.585; -depreciation-life gaming and Burry (LR 0.69) -> 0.49; +volume elasticity resolving FOR elasticity, Google 3.2 quadrillion tokens/mo at 7x YoY (LR 1.6) -> 0.61. Posterior 0.61, matching structural 0.59.

PREMORTEM (de-overlapped): demand/price complex 28%, vintage-specific obsolescence 6%, credit event in the OpenAI/Oracle/private-credit stack 5%, accounting or narrative failure 8%, exogenous 3% = ~50% failure. Both failure and success narratives are easy to write, arguing for a wide interval near 0.5-0.6.

BIAS/RESOLUTION: reversal test passes (a 4x price FALL would have moved me to ~0.40; I applied the symmetric LR up). Scope sensitivity passes ($500B vintage -> 0.85; $3T -> 0.35). Mild status quo bias from extrapolating perpetual scarcity: -2. Resolution mechanics net -4: "not written down" is a low bar for hyperscalers with $500B+ combined operating cash flow (+), but consensus is already skeptical, analysts do headline ROIC not clean vintage accounting so any 2027-29 correction poisons the retrospective even if 2024-26 was genuinely fine (-), the criterion is a conjunction (-), and end-2030 is early since the 2026 tranche still has 1-2 years of life. 0.61 - 0.05 = 0.56.

The highest-leverage single node is OpenAI's solvency: it is the counterparty behind a large share of the contracted backlog that protects the merchant slice, loses $21B/yr, and just cut its 2030 compute plan ~45%. If those commitments restructure, the contracts protecting the vintage evaporate and my estimate drops to ~0.30.
reference_classes: Fiber/telecom capex vintage 1996-2001 (FAIL — ~3% lit capacity, capacity ~100x demand, mass bankruptcies; the canonical bear analogy, but distinguished by ~100% utilization and rising prices in the AI case)
Hyperscaler cloud capex vintage 2010-2020 and 2018-2022 (PASS — same owners, same asset class, contracted/utilized)
US shale capex 2010-2019 (FAIL — ~$300B cumulative FCF destruction, though the earliest best-acreage vintages cleared)
4G/LTE network capex 2010-2014 (PASS — demand elasticity absorbed capacity) vs 5G capex 2019-2023 (FAIL — flat ARPU, no revenue uplift)
Railroad buildout 1870s-1890s and utility nuclear 1970s-80s (FAIL for investors — assets used forever, capital never earned back, stranded-cost write-downs)
Amazon fulfillment capex 2015-2021 (PASS through 2020, 2021 vintage self-admitted overbuild — a vintage-discrimination precedent)
Leading-edge semiconductor fab vintages (PASS for the technology leader, FAIL for laggards — winner-take-most, mirrors the OpenAI/Anthropic demand concentration)

Early-vintage subclass across all booms: the first vintage into a shortage systematically outperforms the boom average because its cash flows are front-loaded into the years it dominates installed capacity
key_uncertainties: OpenAI counterparty solvency — the highest-leverage node. It anchors a large share of the take-or-pay backlog protecting the merchant slice (60% of vintage dollars), loses $20.9B/yr, says it won't be cash-flow positive until 2030, and already cut its 2030 compute plan from $1.4T to $600-750B. A restructuring of those commitments would strip the contractual umbrella and drop my estimate to ~0.30.

How much of the vintage is genuinely contracted at 2025-26 scarcity prices versus exposed to merchant spot rates. My merchant-rate DCF gives ~$1.15T of lifetime revenue against a ~$2.8T requirement (deeply NPV-negative); the contracted-book correction is what rescues the forecast. I cannot verify the contracted share, its duration, or its price terms from the evidence available.

Timing of supply catch-up relative to the 2026 tranche's payback window (2027-2032). The 2026 tranche is 56% of vintage dollars and its payback straddles the analysts' earliest broad-oversupply estimates (~2028). Power interconnect queues (ERCOT 143.5GW vs 85.9GW peak, ~55-month waits) may structurally delay convergence past the payback window — or may not.

Demand elasticity, Thompson's own flagged uncertainty. Token volumes are growing 5-7x/yr against ~40x/yr constant-quality price deflation; revenue is following the frontier tier, not the commodity tier. Whether agentic workloads keep absorbing supply faster than efficiency gains arrive determines everything, and OpenAI's missed internal targets is the first crack.

Run-rate versus recognized revenue. Anthropic's $1B-to-$47B ramp is the most extrapolation-prone figure in the evidence set; it recognized only $4.5B in 2025 against a $9B exit run-rate. If the gap between company-stated run-rates and audited revenue widens, my 2030 revenue path is materially too high.

Resolution ambiguity in the consensus channel. Analysts do headline ROIC, not clean vintage-level NPV accounting. A 2027-29 correction driven by the far larger 2027-2030 vintages would likely produce a negative retrospective on 'the AI capex boom' without discriminating the 2024-26 vintage that may genuinely have cleared its cost of capital.

Whether hyperscalers shorten depreciable lives or take impairments. Amazon's 6-to-5-year reversal citing AI pace is the leading indicator; Burry's $176B understatement claim is the bear anchor. An explicit write-down resolves NO on the second conjunct even if cash economics worked.

Whether Google's and Meta's first-party AI capex (~22% of the vintage), justified by ad-ranking and search-franchise defense rather than rental revenue, will be credited by analysts as NPV-positive or dismissed as unattributable.

CONSENSUS IDENTIFIED: The digest's framing (Cahn's revenue gap, Bain's $800B shortfall, Morgan Stanley's $1.5T financing gap, Burry, SemiAnalysis negative-NPV, Epoch's 3.9yr chip life, OpenAI cutting its compute target) implies a modestly bearish consensus: the 2024-26 vintage probably does not clear its hurdle. Sell-side/market consensus in mid-2026 is the opposite (every capex raise tolerated or rewarded). I attacked both.

FERMI: Vintage = ~$1.43T US AI-attributable capex committed 2024 (~$225B) + 2025 (~$430B) + 2026 (~$780B), ~58% short-lived silicon / ~42% shells+power+land. Hurdle = capex / ~0.72 cash-EBITDA margin ~= $2.0T PV, ~$2.6T nominal. Two attribution models disagree sharply and this is the crux. (a) Pro-rata capacity: vintage share of AI revenue decays 85% (2026) to ~15% (2030) because 2027-30 capex compounds; base case yields ~$1.86T vs $2.6T needed = 0.72x coverage, NO; even the bull path only reaches ~1.0x. This is the strongest and least-discussed bear argument. (b) Scarcity-rent: assets deployed into a 100%-sold-out market earn front-loaded economic rents. Sub-vintage P(NPV+): 2024 ~0.88, 2025 ~0.78, 2026 ~0.52 -> dollar-weighted ~0.66, YES. The pro-rata model's flaw is charging this vintage the AVERAGE return of the entire 2024-2030 program when it demonstrably monopolized the rent years.

CONTRARIAN FINDINGS THAT MOVED ME UP: (1) The project's own verification file shows TechCrunch garbled Cahn -- $1.5T is the LIFETIME requirement for a SINGLE year of capex, not an annual run-rate; the circulating bear hurdle is ~half as scary as reported. (2) SemiAnalysis explicitly retracted its "inexorably steep fall" price assumption; H100 1-yr contracts ROSE ~38% Oct-25 to Mar-26 and all three US labs RAISED nominal prices in 2026 -- the negative-NPV finding was a trough snapshot. (3) Token demand growth (5-7x/yr) still exceeds compute-stock growth (3.4x/yr), the inequality generating the rents, unbroken for three years. (4) ~35% of the vintage (all of Meta's $125-145B, plus Google/Amazon internal) earns against internal ad/search/logistics ROI invisible to every "AI revenue" tally -- the gap literature's numerator is structurally too small. (5) ~42% is shells/power/interconnect; with ERCOT at 143GW of requests vs 86GW peak and 55-month waits, that slice may be worth more in 2030 than at cost. (6) $514B Google RPO, ~$80B Microsoft unfulfillable backlog, ~$1T Nvidia visibility -- fiber-1999 was built against a fabricated traffic statistic, not signed contracts; this is the decisive disanalogy with the dominant bear reference class. (7) Every prior gap analysis has been overtaken: Cahn's $200B (2023) and $600B (2024) questions were both answered as AI end revenue went ~$20B to ~$215B; Anthropic beat its own Nov-2025 "$70B in 2028" projection by ~2 years and hit operating profit in Q2 2026.

CONTRARIAN FINDINGS THAT MOVED ME DOWN: the pro-rata arithmetic; the 2026 tranche is 55% of vintage dollars, deploys into the 2027-28 oversupply window, and embeds component-price inflation (~$25B of Microsoft's plan alone); OpenAI's $665B committed spend against a $20.9B operating loss and targets already cut from $1.4T to $600-750B is the most likely single write-down trigger cascading to Oracle/Broadcom/CoreWeave/Stargate; ~$800B of private credit funding 5-7yr tenors against 3-5yr assets.
